questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I'd always felt drawn to California, so the exchange program was a great opportunity to combine exploration of that crazy place with academics. I chose UCLA as my first priority because of its great reputation and faculty in political science in combination with the high quality of life you only get in SoCal (it truly is always sunny!).

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a fantastic stay in every way and could not recommend it highly enough.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The UC system sends you massive amounts of information ahead of arrival, so as long as you read your email, you'll be fine. The only thing I found confusing was whether I was supposed to participate in an orientation program or not (I didn't), and I'm honestly still not sure. Either way you'll be just fine without, but it may be a way to get to know some people.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: No personal assistance, but the Dashew Center (international student office) organized some events with useful information. Just check your email and reach out to them if you have questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Stay at the coop!!! University Cooperative Housing Association (UCHA). You may think it's not for you, since sharing a room with two other people is a daunting prospect for someone who's used to having their own space. The truth is, you will not find anything remotely close to the value for money you get at the coop, and it is an AMAZING place to meet people and make a ton of friends. I was skeptical before arriving, but it turned out to be the best decision I made on the whole stay.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: On-campus housing at UCLA is VERY expensive. The base price is about twice that of the coop, and on top comes a food plan, which is included at the coop. It is not as well maintained as on-campus housing, but it is just as close to campus and the community is much stronger.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I know you're still thinking.... "sharing a room with two random people? In a somewhat neglected concrete building where I even have to work a shift once a week? No thanks, I can find something better!" Well, I tried. Trust me: you can't. ;)

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Enrolling wasn't the most intuitive, but they do provide some resources to guide you through it. The registration process in itself was easy enough, but there are some things that you just have to research ahead of time, such as prerequisites. A major annoyance is that you can't see the syllabus ahead of time; you only have the title and a brief description to work with. You should consider emailing the instructor to ask for the syllabus to help make your decision. Also check out Bruinwalk (website where students review courses).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: They release the course catalog (class planner) at MyUCLA, and then you have some time before your enrollment timeslot. Courses vary a lot in difficulty, exam format, and workload, so do your research ahead of your timeslot.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They send you some guides, but what's more helpful is checking out the courses on your own to make an informed decision.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Mostly successful. As a first-year master student, I was interested in taking at least some graduate courses, which the system doesn't let you by default (the exchange program is an undergraduate program, so you are registered as such in the UC system). You can email professors and ask for permission to enroll anyway, which they will sometimes grant. I ended up with two out of six courses on graduate level, which was OK. The undergrad classes varied a LOT - some were very good, and some less so. One class was a complete mess.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Check out Bruinwalk. Email professors for the course syllabus. If you like a course that's for graduate students, or one that has prerequisites, email the professor and ask for permission to enroll anyway.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Again, it just varies so much from course to course that it's hard to describe. I learned something from every course, but some courses were tedious and disorganized, while others were incredibly rewarding.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The two graduate courses I took were on a high level, even for UCPH. The undergraduate courses I took were generally easier analytically than at UCPH, but not all of them. I guess the general takeaway is that they don't expect you to conduct much independent research work on a high level, but they do encourage you to. You will usually get A's or B's for assignments that would've landed you a 7 at UCPH, but if you want to challenge yourself and submit something solid, you absolutely can.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Courses generally have lectures and discussion sections just like at UCPH. In some courses, attendance is mandatory. They generally require much more work during the quarter than at UCPH, but for the most part they're easier. Be prepared for pen and paper exams!!! Midterms AND finals! I'm a slow handwriter and this genuinely screwed me over in two classes that I otherwise would've received A's in but ended up with B's.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I was away for 1,5 semesters (two quarters).
First quarter (fall): POL SCI 140B: National Institutions: The Presidency; POL SCI 260A: Survey Course in American Politics: Political Parties and Electoral Process; POL SCI 125A: Arms Control and International Security.

Second quarter (winter): GLB HLT 100: Introduction to Global Health; POL SCI 163B: Colonialism, Discourse, and Democracy; PUB PLC C275: Advanced Technology: Public Policy, Regulation, and Law.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
POL SCI 260A with Lynn Vavreck was amazing, perhaps the best course I've had at uni ever. It was approx 10 PhD students and me in a small classroom for three hours every Monday, discussing a ton of great readings on a high level. But don't be shy, you can definitely keep up even though they're PhD (in most cases, they had studied as many years as I had - the university systems are different and in the US PhDs usually don't take a master's degree first).

I liked PUB PLC C275 with professor Zipperstein who is just a darling - very lovable and knowledgeable guy.

POL SCI 140B was super interesting but pretty demanding too. I really learned a lot from this class that I would never learn at UCPH. Highly recommended, just be aware that you have pen and paper midterm and final as well as a 15 page research paper, and that some of the material is pretty complicated.

The other three courses (GLB HLT 100, POL SCI 163B and POL SCI 125A) were not the best. Global Health was interesting but pretty basic yet demanding in terms of workload. Arms Control was a complete mess. Colonialism, Discourse and Democracy was mostly quite boring but in the end I actually turned and learned to enjoy the class. It certainly isn't for everyone, though.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing I can think of.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Prices are generally high in California and LA in particular. Groceries can be very expensive (think 75 DKK for 12 eggs). This is another reason why the coop is such a crazy good offer, you get three meals per day included with your rent. The only food I've bought is while traveling and the occassional night out/hangover treat. You can even pack lunches and take them to uni.

Insurance is expensive obviously, but you should have that covered before leaving. Uber is very expensive. Domestic plane tickets are pretty cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't join in any clubs, but there are so many you'll get dizzy. I did try to join the backpacking club but ended up just organizing the trips myself with my friends.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Every kind you can imagine... just go to the huge student fare in week 0 and see what you like!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Use the amazing facilities! UCLA has 7 swimming pools on campus, a bunch of professional sports stadiums and tennis courts and free or cheap learning opportunities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
This is VERY important! GO SEE CALIFORNIA! The national parks are amazing: Sequoia, Yosemite, Death Valley, Joshua Tree, ... Also make sure to take a trip eastward to Utah and Arizona, their parks are even better. I LOVED Zion national park (get the permit for the Angels Landing trail <33), and Monument Valley, Arches, Bryce, Grand Canyon are all super cool. And don't forget the iconic Pacific Coast Highway for a sublime road trip up toward San Francisco - Big Sur which you'll see on the way is magical. Last but not least, go to Hawaii!!! Check Google Flights for cheap tickets (I got a two-island return ticket for less than 300 USD). It's a unique experience that I wish I could do every year. Stay at the hostels and go on their daily tours (on Maui they're free). 

Overall, traveling was one of the main things I did because so many incredible places with so much variation are super accessible from LA. Just make sure you have some money saved up for it... (take that SU lån -- stay at the coop -- apply for a bunch of grants -- don't save on travel!!)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy! Americans are famously open, and if you stay at the coop, which you should, you'll get a bunch of friends in no time. The only thing is sharing a room, that took some time for me but I ended up becoming really close with my roommates and kind of enjoying that way of living. Also, you'll definitely struggle getting around if you don't have a car, that's just how it is. UCLA gives you free public transport in the whole city, but it's extremely poorly connected. I bought a car and used it alllll the time. It was cheap! But it does require a lot of work in terms of insurance, parking, maintenance, etc. If you have the dream of driving through Beverly Hills in a convertible, you absolutely can -- I got a 2006 Toyota Solara for 2700 USD that worked close to flawlessly and that I sold for the same price at the end of my stay. Worth all the trouble and much more. Having to beg for spots in other people's cars just gets tiring very fast, and honestly driving is so much more enjoyable in the US.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Stay at the coop :=)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I missed walking around to explore. I felt pretty constrained in my choices before I got my car, and even then, I still missed walking. LA is not a European city, you cannot walk between neighborhoods. For that reason getting to know LA is super difficult. Some neighborhoods are fine for walking (Santa Monica, Venice, West Hollywood, Westwood and of course the tourist spots), but getting to them is tough without a car.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. Stay at the coop. 2. Buy a car. 3. Travel!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: DON'T buy the super expensive UC SHIP insurance. Get the much cheaper ISO Care student health insurance and get a waiver for UC SHIP. I also bought a travel insurance on top from Gouda.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Traveling with all the friends I made at the coop.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Going back home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
